at tabe.explanation: "At tabe" means "to lose" a game, a fight or a bet: "Vi taber kampen" (We lose the match). It can also mean "to drop" something: "Jeg tabte min telefon" (I dropped my phone). For losing an item you cannot find, use "at miste" (to lose something).

sentence.da: Pas på, du skal ikke **tabe** glasset på gulvet!
sentence.en: Careful, don't drop the glass on the floor!

at tage.explanation: "At tage" means "to take", but Danish uses it more widely than English. You "tager" (take) a bus, a train, a photo, a shower or a day off. It can also mean "to go": "Jeg tager til København" (I am going to Copenhagen). "Tag!" means "Take it!" or "Here you go!".

sentence.da: Du kan **tage** en kage fra bordet.
sentence.en: You can take a cake from the table.

at tage af.explanation: "At tage af" means "to take off" clothes: "Jeg tager jakken af" (I take my jacket off). The little word "af" (off) goes after the thing you take off.

related.en: to put on, to gain weight

sentence.da: Her er varmt. Du kan godt **tage af**, hvis du vil.
sentence.en: It is warm here. You can take your coat off if you like.

at tage bad.explanation: "At tage bad" means "to take a shower" or "to have a bath", and there is no "et" (a) before "bad" in this phrase. For a shower in particular, say "at tage brusebad" (to take a shower); for a soak in the tub, "at tage et karbad" (to take a bath in a tub).

sentence.da: Efter løbeturen vil jeg **tage bad** og vaske håret.
sentence.en: After the run I want to take a shower and wash my hair.

at tage bussen.explanation: "At tage bussen" means "to take the bus" or "to go by bus". Danish uses "at tage" (to take) for ways of travelling, so you also say "at tage toget" (to take the train).

sentence.da: Min bil er i stykker, så jeg må **tage bussen** til arbejde.
sentence.en: My car is broken, so I have to take the bus to work.

at tage et billede.explanation: "At tage et billede" means "to take a picture". "At tage et foto" (to take a photo) means the same. To say what is in the picture, use "af" (of): "tage et billede af maden" (to take a picture of the food).

sentence.da: Du er så smuk! Må jeg **tage et billede** af dig?
sentence.en: You look so pretty! May I take a picture of you?

at tage hjem.explanation: "At tage hjem" means "to go home", usually leaving a place such as work or a party. Normally "tage" means "to take", but in this phrase it means "to go".

sentence.da: Det er sent, så vi vil **tage hjem** nu.
sentence.en: It is late, so we want to go home now.

at tage medicin.explanation: "At tage medicin" means "to take medicine". "Medicin" has no "en" or "et" (a) in front of it when you mean medicine in general. The same verb is used for a pill: "at tage en tablet" (to take a tablet).

sentence.da: Jeg er syg, så jeg skal **tage medicin** to gange om dagen.
sentence.en: I am sick, so I have to take medicine twice a day.

at tage på ferie.explanation: "At tage på ferie" means "to go on vacation". You can add where you go: "tage på ferie til Spanien" (to go on vacation to Spain). To say you are already on vacation, use "at være på ferie" (to be on vacation).

sentence.da: Vi vil **tage på ferie** til Spanien, hvor solen skinner.
sentence.en: We want to go on vacation to Spain, where the sun shines.

at tage toget.explanation: "At tage toget" means "to take the train" or "to go by train". Danish uses "at tage" (to take) with the type of transport, so you also say "at tage taxaen" (to take the taxi). The past form "tog" looks the same as "et tog" (a train), so the context tells you which is meant.

sentence.da: Toget kører hurtigt, så jeg vil **tage toget** til København.
sentence.en: The train goes fast, so I want to take the train to Copenhagen.

at takke.explanation: "At takke" means "to thank": "Jeg vil gerne takke dig" (I would like to thank you). It sounds a bit more formal. In daily life people simply say "tak" (thanks) or "tusind tak" (thank you very much).

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne **takke** dig for hjælpen.
sentence.en: I would like to thank you for the help.

at tale.explanation: "At tale" means "to speak", for a language or a speech: "Jeg taler dansk" (I speak Danish). For casual chatting, Danes prefer "at snakke" (to chat, to talk). You say "at tale med nogen" (to speak with someone) and "at tale om noget" (to talk about something).

sentence.da: Kan du **tale** dansk?
sentence.en: Can you speak Danish?

at tale med.explanation: "At tale med" means "to talk to" or "to talk with" someone. The little word "med" (with) comes after it: "tale med nogen" (to talk to someone). It is common on the phone: "Kan jeg tale med Anna?" (Can I speak to Anna?).

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne **tale med** dig.
sentence.en: I would like to talk to you.

at tale om.explanation: "At tale om" means "to talk about" a topic: "Vi taler om vejret" (We talk about the weather). It is a bit more formal than "at snakke om" (to chat about), but you can use either in everyday life.

sentence.da: Vi vil **tale om** vejret, fordi det er så koldt.
sentence.en: We want to talk about the weather, because it is so cold.

at tisse.explanation: "At tisse" means "to pee". It is an informal, everyday word used by children, and by adults among friends and family: "Jeg skal tisse" (I need to pee). In a polite setting, say "Jeg skal på toilettet" (I need to go to the toilet).

sentence.da: Barnet drikker meget, og nu skal det **tisse**.
sentence.en: The child drinks a lot, and now it needs to pee.

at tjekke.explanation: "At tjekke" means "to check", and it is borrowed from English. You can check your phone, the time, or whether something is right. A more formal word is "at kontrollere" (to check, to inspect), and "at undersøge" (to investigate) is for looking into something more deeply.

sentence.da: Jeg skal lige **tjekke** min telefon.
sentence.en: I just need to check my phone.

at tro.explanation: "At tro" means "to believe" or "to think something is probably true": "Jeg tror, det er rigtigt" (I think it is right). It is also used for faith: "at tro på Gud" (to believe in God). "At synes" (to think, to have an opinion) is for your own taste, while "at tro" is more of a guess about facts.

sentence.da: Jeg kan ikke **tro**, at han er her.
sentence.en: I can't believe he is here.

at trække vejret.explanation: "At trække vejret" means "to breathe". Literally it is "to pull the breath", with "vejret" meaning "the breath". The same word "vejret" also means "the weather", but the phrase makes the meaning clear.

sentence.da: Du skal **trække vejret** dybt, siger lægen.
sentence.en: You must breathe deeply, says the doctor.

at træne.explanation: "At træne" means "to train" or "to work out", and also "to practise": "Jeg træner tre gange om ugen" (I work out three times a week). It is used for sports and the gym, and for practising a skill: "træne dansk" (to practise Danish).

sentence.da: Jeg vil **træne** tre gange om ugen.
sentence.en: I want to work out three times a week.

at tælle.explanation: "At tælle" means "to count": "Jeg tæller til ti" (I count to ten). Its past forms "jeg talte" and "jeg har talt" are exactly the same as for "at tale" (to speak), so the context tells you which is meant.

sentence.da: Jeg kan **tælle**: en, to, tre, fire.
sentence.en: I can count: one, two, three, four.

at tænde.explanation: "At tænde" means "to turn on" a light and also "to light" a candle, a fire or a cigarette: "Tænd lyset" (Turn on the light). For a TV, a radio or running water, Danes usually say "tænde for" instead. Do not mix it up with "at tænke" (to think), which looks almost the same.

sentence.da: Det er mørkt, så jeg vil **tænde** lyset.
sentence.en: It is dark, so I want to turn on the light.

at tænde for.explanation: "At tænde for" means "to turn on" something that runs or plays, such as the TV, the radio, the water or the heating. For a light, a candle or a fire, plain "tænde" is the usual choice: "tænde lyset" (turn on the light), though "tænde for lyset" is also heard when you flip a light switch.

sentence.da: Det er koldt, så jeg vil **tænde for** varmen.
sentence.en: It is cold, so I want to turn on the heating.

at tænke.explanation: "At tænke" means "to think" in the sense of using your mind: "Jeg tænker på dig" (I am thinking of you). It goes with "på" (about). It is not the word for giving an opinion, which is "at synes" (to think, to have an opinion). "Lad mig tænke" means "Let me think".

sentence.da: Det er et svært spørgsmål, så jeg må **tænke** lidt.
sentence.en: It is a hard question, so I have to think a bit.

en t-shirt.explanation: "En t-shirt" means "a t-shirt". It is borrowed from English. To say you are wearing one, use "have ... på" (literally "have ... on").

sentence.da: Det er varmt, så jeg har kun en blå **t-shirt** på.
sentence.en: It is warm, so I am only wearing a blue t-shirt.

en tallerken.explanation: "En tallerken" means "a plate". At the table you can ask for "en tallerken til" (one more plate). The stress is at the start: "TAL-ler-ken".

sentence.da: Der er mad på min **tallerken**.
sentence.en: There is food on my plate.

en tand.explanation: "En tand" means "a tooth". The plural is "tænder" (teeth), where "a" becomes "æ". "At børste tænder" means "to brush teeth".

sentence.da: Jeg har ondt i en **tand**, så jeg skal til tandlægen.
sentence.en: I have a pain in a tooth, so I am going to the dentist.

en tandlæge.explanation: "En tandlæge" means "a dentist", made from "tand" (tooth) and "læge" (doctor). You say "Jeg skal til tandlægen" (I am going to the dentist), and the same pattern works for "til lægen" (to the doctor).

sentence.da: Min **tandlæge** kigger på mine tænder.
sentence.en: My dentist looks at my teeth.

en tante.explanation: "En tante" means "an aunt", the sister of a parent or the wife of an uncle. More exactly, "faster" is your father's sister and "moster" your mother's sister, but "tante" works for both.

sentence.da: Min **tante** er min mors søster.
sentence.en: My aunt is my mother's sister.

en taske.explanation: "En taske" means "a bag" with a handle or strap, such as a handbag or school bag. A thin plastic shop bag is "en pose" (a plastic bag) instead. Words can go in front: "en håndtaske" (a handbag), "en skoletaske" (a school bag).

sentence.da: Jeg har bøger i min **taske**, og jeg bærer den til skole.
sentence.en: I have books in my bag, and I carry it to school.

en taxa.explanation: "En taxa" means "a taxi". You say "med en taxa" (by taxi) and "at bestille en taxa" (to book a taxi).

sentence.da: Vi tager en **taxa**, og chaufføren kører os til lufthavnen.
sentence.en: We take a taxi, and the driver takes us to the airport.

en taxachauffør.explanation: "En taxachauffør" means "a taxi driver", built from "taxa" (taxi) and "chauffør" (driver). You can tell the driver where to go with "Til banegården, tak" (To the railway station, please).

sentence.da: Min far er **taxachauffør** og kører rundt i byen hele dagen.
sentence.en: My father is a taxi driver and drives around the city all day.

en tegnebog.explanation: "En tegnebog" means "a wallet", the kind that holds banknotes and cards. It is a bit more formal than "en pung" (a wallet), though both are used.

sentence.da: Han tager penge og et kort ud af sin **tegnebog**.
sentence.en: He takes money and a card out of his wallet.

en telefon.explanation: "En telefon" means "a phone". A mobile phone is "en mobiltelefon" or, more often, just "en mobil". To phone someone, say "at ringe til" (to call) that person: "Jeg ringer til dig" (I will call you).

sentence.da: Min **telefon** ringer, og jeg tager den.
sentence.en: My phone is ringing, and I pick it up.

en temperatur.explanation: "En temperatur" means "a temperature", how hot or cold something is. For a high body temperature when you are ill, say "at have feber" (to have a fever).

sentence.da: Med en **temperatur** på tyve grader er det en varm dag.
sentence.en: With a temperature of twenty degrees it is a warm day.

en tid.explanation: "En tid" means "time" in general: "Jeg har tid" means "I have time". Danish splits what English calls "time": "en gang" is one occasion (once, twice) and "en time" is an hour. To ask the clock time, say "Hvad er klokken?" (What time is it?).

sentence.da: Jeg har ikke **tid** nu, for jeg skal på arbejde.
sentence.en: I do not have time now, because I have to go to work.

forms.da: Jeg har en tid hos lægen.
Jeg skal have en tid hos lægen.
forms.en: I need to get a doctor's appointment.

en tid hos lægen.explanation: "En tid hos lægen" means "a doctor's appointment", literally "a time at the doctor". "En tid" works for any booked time, such as at the dentist or hairdresser. To book one, say "at bestille en tid" (to book an appointment).

sentence.da: Jeg har en **tid hos lægen** klokken ti, fordi jeg er syg.
sentence.en: I have a doctor's appointment at ten o'clock, because I am sick.

en tiger.explanation: "En tiger" means "a tiger", spelled almost like the English word. The "g" is not pronounced, so it sounds roughly like "TEE-uh".

sentence.da: Børnene ser en stor **tiger** med striber i zoo.
sentence.en: The children see a big tiger with stripes at the zoo.

en time.explanation: "En time" means "an hour". It also means a lesson or class, so "en dansktime" is a Danish lesson. "Om en time" means "in an hour". For time in general, say "tid" (time).

sentence.da: Der er tres minutter i en **time**.
sentence.en: There are sixty minutes in an hour.

en ting.explanation: "En ting" means "a thing". The plural looks the same as the singular, so "mange ting" means "many things". It is handy when you do not know the right name: "Hvad er det for en ting?" (What is that thing?).

sentence.da: I min taske har jeg mange **ting**: en bog, en telefon og en nøgle.
sentence.en: In my bag I have many things: a book, a phone and a key.

en tjener.explanation: "En tjener" means "a waiter", for men and women alike. It can also mean "a servant".

sentence.da: Jeg bestiller mad, og en **tjener** kommer med menuen.
sentence.en: I order food, and a waiter comes with the menu.

en togbillet.explanation: "En togbillet" means "a train ticket", built from "tog" (train) and "billet" (ticket). Other tickets work the same way: "en busbillet" is a bus ticket.

sentence.da: Jeg har købt en **togbillet**, så jeg kan køre med toget til Odense.
sentence.en: I have bought a train ticket so I can travel by train to Odense.

en togstation.explanation: "En togstation" means "a train station", built from "tog" (train) and "station" (station). You say "på togstationen" for "at the train station".

sentence.da: Toget holder ved en **togstation**, og vi stiger af.
sentence.en: The train stops at a train station, and we get off.

en tomat.explanation: "En tomat" means "a tomato". Danish often joins words into one: "tomatsuppe" is tomato soup and "tomatsovs" is tomato sauce.

sentence.da: Jeg skærer en rød **tomat** til salaten.
sentence.en: I cut a red tomato for the salad.

en tommelfinger.explanation: "En tommelfinger" means "a thumb". "Tommelfinger op" means "thumbs up". Danish says "the thumb" where English says "my thumb": "Jeg har ondt i tommelfingeren" means "I have a pain in the thumb", that is, "my thumb hurts".

sentence.da: Jeg har slået min **tommelfinger** med en hammer, og den gør ondt.
sentence.en: I hit my thumb with a hammer, and it hurts.

en trøje.explanation: "En trøje" means "a sweater" or "a jumper". Danes also use it for other tops, such as "en fodboldtrøje" (a football shirt).

sentence.da: Det er koldt, så jeg tager min **trøje** på.
sentence.en: It is cold, so I put on my sweater.

en tunge.explanation: "En tunge" means "a tongue", the one in your mouth. A phrase to know is "at række tunge" (to stick out your tongue).

sentence.da: Lægen sagde: Vis mig din **tunge**.
sentence.en: The doctor said: Show me your tongue.

en tur.explanation: "En tur" means "a trip" or "a turn". "At gå en tur" is "to go for a walk", "at tage på tur" is "to go on a trip", and "Det er din tur" means "It is your turn". A longer, bigger journey is "en rejse" (a journey).

sentence.da: Vi går en **tur** i parken.
sentence.en: We are going for a walk in the park.

en tysker.explanation: "En tysker" means "a German", a person from Germany. The word is used for both men and women. You can say either "Jeg er tysker" or "Jeg er tysk" (I am German).

sentence.da: Hun er **tysker** og bor i Tyskland.
sentence.en: She is a German and lives in Germany.

en tå.explanation: "En tå" means "a toe". Danish often says "the toe" where English says "my toe": "Jeg slog tåen" means "I hit my toe". A big toe is "en stortå".

sentence.da: Jeg slog min **tå** mod døren, og det gjorde ondt.
sentence.en: I hit my toe on the door and it hurt.

en tøjbutik.explanation: "En tøjbutik" means "a clothing store". It is made from "tøj" (clothes) and "butik" (shop), and Danish often joins words like this: "skobutik" (shoe store).

sentence.da: Jeg køber en trøje og bukser i en **tøjbutik**.
sentence.en: I buy a sweater and trousers in a clothing store.

et tal.explanation: "Et tal" means "a number", like 5 or 12, in the sense of a figure you count with. For a phone number or house number Danes use "et nummer" instead.

sentence.da: Fem er et lille **tal**.
sentence.en: Five is a small number.

et telefonnummer.explanation: "Et telefonnummer" means "a phone number", built from "telefon" (phone) and "nummer" (number). "Hvad er dit telefonnummer?" means "What is your phone number?".

sentence.da: Jeg kan ikke ringe til dig, for jeg har ikke dit **telefonnummer**.
sentence.en: I cannot call you, because I do not have your phone number.

et tilbud.explanation: "Et tilbud" means "an offer" or "a deal". In a shop, "på tilbud" means "on sale", at a lower price for a short time.

sentence.da: Der er et godt **tilbud** på kaffe i dag.
sentence.en: There is a good deal on coffee today.

et tog.explanation: "Et tog" means "a train". To say you go by train, Danes say "at tage toget", literally "to take the train": "Jeg tager toget" means "I take the train".

sentence.da: Vi venter på perronen, og vores **tog** kommer om fem minutter.
sentence.en: We wait on the platform and our train comes in five minutes.

et toilet.explanation: "Et toilet" means "a toilet", and also the room that has one. "Hvor er toilettet?" means "Where is the toilet?" and is how you ask for the restroom. On the doors you see "Herrer" (men) and "Damer" (women).

sentence.da: Jeg skal på **toilet** og vaske hænder.
sentence.en: I am going to the toilet to wash my hands.

et træ.explanation: "Et træ" means "a tree", and also "wood" as a material: "et bord af træ" means "a table made of wood". For a large group of trees Danes say "en skov" (a forest).

sentence.da: Et stort **træ** med grønne blade står i haven.
sentence.en: A big tree with green leaves stands in the garden.

et tv.explanation: "Et tv" means "a TV" and is said "te-ve". Watching TV is "at se tv", literally "to see TV". The longer word "et fjernsyn" (a television) means the same.

sentence.da: Jeg sidder i sofaen og ser **tv**.
sentence.en: I sit on the sofa and watch TV.

et tørklæde.explanation: "Et tørklæde" means "a scarf", something you wrap around your neck or head. The second half is "klæde" (a cloth), which you also see in "et håndklæde" (a towel).

sentence.da: Det er koldt, så tag dit **tørklæde** på.
sentence.en: It is cold, so put your scarf on.

tak.explanation: "Tak" means "thanks", and Danish also uses it for "please": "ja tak" is "yes, please" and "Kaffe, tak" is "Coffee, please". You answer thanks with "selv tak" (you're welcome).

sentence.da: **Tak** for gaven, den er flot!
sentence.en: Thanks for the gift, it is beautiful!

tak for det.explanation: "Tak for det" means "thanks for that", a friendly way to thank someone for something that just happened, like advice, help or a small favour. It is more casual than "mange tak" (thank you very much). You can put other things after "tak for": "Tak for kaffen" means "Thanks for the coffee".

sentence.da: **Tak for det**, det var rart!
sentence.en: Thanks for that, it was nice!

forms.da: Tak for i dag, vi ses.

tak for i dag.explanation: "Tak for i dag" means "thanks for today", said when you part after a day together, such as work, a course or a meeting. Change "i dag" to "i aften" (tonight) for an evening, or say "tak for sidst" (thanks for last time) when you meet again.

sentence.da: **Tak for i dag**, det var en god dag.
sentence.en: Thanks for today, it was a good day.

forms.da: Tak for mad, det var lækkert.
forms.en: Thanks for the meal, it was delicious.

tak for mad.explanation: "Tak for mad" means "thanks for the meal" ("mad" is food). You say it at the end of a meal to thank whoever made the food. The reply is "velbekomme" (you're welcome, said about food).

sentence.da: **Tak for mad**, det var rigtig lækkert.
sentence.en: Thanks for the meal, it was really delicious.

forms.da: Jeg forstår, når du taler langsomt
forms.en: I understand when you speak slowly

tal langsomt.explanation: "Tal langsomt" means "speak slowly". Adding "tak" (please) makes it polite, and "Kan du tale langsommere?" (Can you speak more slowly?) is even softer.

sentence.da: Jeg forstår ikke, **tal langsomt**, tak.
sentence.en: I do not understand, speak slowly, please.

forms.en: I only speak a little Danish.

taler du engelsk?.explanation: "Taler du engelsk?" means "Do you speak English?". It is polite to try a little Danish first: "Jeg taler lidt dansk" (I speak a little Danish). To ask several people say "Taler I engelsk?" (Do you all speak English?), and for one person you address very formally, "Taler De engelsk?" (Do you speak English, sir or madam?).

sentence.da: Undskyld, **taler du engelsk?**
sentence.en: Excuse me, do you speak English?

tandpine.explanation: "Tandpine" means "toothache". It is built from "tand" (tooth) and "pine" (pain). You can also say "Jeg har ondt i tanden" (literally "I have pain in the tooth").

sentence.da: Jeg har **tandpine** og skal til tandlægen.
sentence.en: I have a toothache and need to go to the dentist.

te.explanation: "Te" means "tea". It is said like English "tay", not like "tee". Do not mix it up with "ti" (ten), which is said like "tee".

sentence.da: Jeg drikker varm **te** med citron.
sentence.en: I drink hot tea with lemon.

tennis.explanation: "Tennis" means "tennis". You play it with "at spille" (to play) and leave out "en": "Hun spiller tennis hver torsdag" (She plays tennis every Thursday).

sentence.da: Vi spiller **tennis** med en bold på en bane.
sentence.en: We play tennis with a ball on a court.

ti.explanation: "Ti" means "ten", said like "tee". Do not mix it up with "tid" (time), which has a "d" on the end and sounds different.

sentence.da: Efter ni kommer **ti**, og efter ti kommer elleve.
sentence.en: After nine comes ten, and after ten comes eleven.

tidlig.explanation: "Tidlig" means "early". To say you do something early, Danish uses "tidligt": "Jeg står tidligt op" (I get up early).

sentence.da: Klokken fem om morgenen er meget **tidlig**.
sentence.en: Five o'clock in the morning is very early.

tidligt.explanation: "Tidligt" means "early" when it says when something happens: "Jeg står tidligt op" (I get up early). To describe a thing, use "tidlig", as in "en tidlig morgen" (an early morning).

sentence.da: Jeg skal stå **tidligt** op i morgen, klokken fem.
sentence.en: I have to get up early tomorrow, at five o'clock.

tiende.explanation: "Tiende" means "tenth". It is used for dates: "den tiende juni" is "the tenth of June". In writing you can use "10." with a dot after the number.

sentence.da: Efter den niende kommer den **tiende**.
sentence.en: After the ninth comes the tenth.

til.explanation: "Til" means "to": it shows where you are going or who something is for. It is also used in times like "til jul" (at Christmas).

sentence.da: Jeg rejser **til** Aarhus i morgen.
sentence.en: I am travelling to Aarhus tomorrow.

forms.en: The bank is on the right.

til højre.explanation: "Til højre" means "to the right", or "on the right". It is used for directions: "Drej til højre" (Turn right).

sentence.da: Gå ligeud og drej **til højre**.
sentence.en: Go straight ahead and turn right.

forms.en: The post office is on the left.

til venstre.explanation: "Til venstre" means "to the left", or "on the left". It is used for directions: "Drej til venstre" (Turn left).

sentence.da: Du skal dreje **til venstre**, ikke til højre.
sentence.en: You have to turn left, not right.

tilbage.explanation: "Tilbage" means "back", as in going or giving back: "Hun går tilbage" (She goes back). It also means "left over": "Der er to tilbage" (There are two left). For the body part, use "ryg" (back).

sentence.da: Jeg går nu, men jeg kommer snart **tilbage**.
sentence.en: I am going now, but I will be back soon.

tillykke.explanation: "Tillykke" means "congratulations". Add "med" (on) and what you are celebrating: "tillykke med bilen" (congratulations on the car).

sentence.da: **Tillykke** med din nye lejlighed!
sentence.en: Congratulations on your new flat!

tillykke med fødselsdagen.explanation: "Tillykke med fødselsdagen" means "happy birthday", literally "congratulations with the birthday". It can be shortened to "tillykke med dagen" (congratulations on the day).

sentence.da: Her er en kage og en gave. **Tillykke med fødselsdagen**, Anna!
sentence.en: Here is a cake and a present. Happy birthday, Anna!

tirsdag.explanation: "Tirsdag" means "Tuesday". Day names are written with a small letter in Danish. "På tirsdag" means "on Tuesday" (the coming one), and "om tirsdagen" or "hver tirsdag" means "every Tuesday".

sentence.da: I dag er det mandag, og i morgen er det **tirsdag**.
sentence.en: Today it is Monday, and tomorrow it is Tuesday.

to.explanation: "To" means "two". It is the same before any word, so "to biler" (two cars) and "to huse" (two houses) both work. In numbers like 22 the ones come first: "toogtyve" is literally "two-and-twenty".

sentence.da: En, **to**, tre, fire!
sentence.en: One, two, three, four!

to gange.explanation: "To gange" means "twice", literally "two times". "En gang" is "once" (one time), and with any bigger number the word becomes "gange".

sentence.da: Én gang, **to gange**, tre gange!
sentence.en: Once, twice, three times!

tolv.explanation: "Tolv" means "twelve". The "v" at the end is not pronounced, so it sounds a bit like "tol".

sentence.da: Efter elleve kommer **tolv**.
sentence.en: After eleven comes twelve.

tom.explanation: "Tom" means "empty", for a bottle, a room, a street or a plate. The opposite is "fuld" (full), which can also mean "drunk" when it describes a person.

sentence.da: Flasken er **tom**, der er ikke mere vand i den.
sentence.en: The bottle is empty, there is no more water in it.

torsdag.explanation: "Torsdag" means "Thursday". Day names are written with a small letter in Danish. "På torsdag" means "on Thursday" (the coming one) and "om torsdagen" means "on Thursdays". Do not mix it up with "tirsdag" (Tuesday), which looks similar.

sentence.da: I morgen er det onsdag, og dagen efter er det **torsdag**.
sentence.en: Tomorrow is Wednesday, and the day after is Thursday.

travl.explanation: "Travl" means "busy", for a person, a day, a street or a shop. "Jeg har det travlt" means "I am busy" or "I am in a hurry".

sentence.da: Jeg har meget at lave i dag. Det er en **travl** dag.
sentence.en: I have a lot to do today. It is a busy day.

tre.explanation: "Tre" means "three", and it stays the same before any word. The Danish "r" is softer and further back in the throat than the English one.

sentence.da: Jeg har **tre** æbler: et rødt, et grønt og et gult.
sentence.en: I have three apples: a red one, a green one and a yellow one.

tredive.explanation: "Tredive" means "thirty". In numbers like 31 the ones come first: "enogtredive" is literally "one-and-thirty".

sentence.da: Ti, tyve, **tredive**, fyrre.
sentence.en: Ten, twenty, thirty, forty.

tredje.explanation: "Tredje" means "third". It is used for dates too: "den tredje oktober" is "the third of October".

sentence.da: Først kommer den første, så den anden og så den **tredje**.
sentence.en: First comes the first, then the second and then the third.

tres.explanation: "Tres" means "sixty". It is short for the older word "tresindstyve", literally "three times twenty".

sentence.da: Halvtreds, **tres**, halvfjerds.
sentence.en: Fifty, sixty, seventy.

tretten.explanation: "Tretten" means "thirteen". It is built from "tre" (three) and "-ten" (ten). Watch the spelling: it has "tt" in the middle.

sentence.da: Tolv, **tretten**, fjorten.
sentence.en: Twelve, thirteen, fourteen.

trist.explanation: "Trist" means "sad". It can describe a person who feels sad ("Jeg er trist", I am sad) and also things that are sad or dull, such as a film or grey weather. For feeling upset, "ked af det" (upset) is also very common.

sentence.da: Hun græder, fordi filmen er så **trist**.
sentence.en: She is crying because the film is so sad.

trusser.explanation: "Trusser" means "panties" or "briefs", women's underwear, and it is normally used in the plural. For men's underwear the usual word is "underbukser", and "undertøj" means underwear in general.

sentence.da: Hun tager **trusser**, bukser og en trøje på.
sentence.en: She puts on panties, trousers and a sweater.

træt.explanation: "Træt" means "tired". "Jeg er træt" means "I am tired". With "af" (of) it means "fed up with": "træt af det" (fed up with it).

sentence.da: Jeg sov kun tre timer, så nu er jeg meget **træt**.
sentence.en: I only slept three hours, so now I am very tired.

tung.explanation: "Tung" means "heavy", for a bag, a box or shopping. It also describes food that feels heavy in the stomach ("tung mad", heavy food) and a heavy mood.

sentence.da: Kufferten er så **tung**, at jeg ikke kan løfte den.
sentence.en: The suitcase is so heavy that I cannot lift it.

turkis.explanation: "Turkis" means "turquoise", a blue-green color. Note the spelling: Danish has a "k" where English has "qu".

sentence.da: Når blå og grøn blandes, bliver farven **turkis**.
sentence.en: When blue and green are mixed, the color becomes turquoise.

tusind.explanation: "Tusind" means "a thousand". It is used for amounts, prices and distances: "fem tusind" is "five thousand". Years are said with hundreds instead: 1999 is "nitten hundrede og nioghalvfems" (nineteen hundred and ninety-nine).

sentence.da: Ti gange hundrede er **tusind**.
sentence.en: Ten times a hundred is a thousand.

forms.en: Thanks a lot for your help.

forms.da: Tusind tak, det var pænt af dig.
forms.en: Thanks a lot, that was kind of you.

tusind tak.explanation: "Tusind tak" means "thanks a lot", literally "a thousand thanks". It is a little warmer than "mange tak" (thank you very much). Use it when someone has really helped you.

sentence.da: Du har hjulpet mig så meget. **Tusind tak**!
sentence.en: You have helped me so much. Thanks a lot!

tyk.explanation: "Tyk" means "thick", such as a thick book or a thick coat. About a person it means "fat" and can sound rude, so be careful.

sentence.da: Bogen har mange sider, så den er meget **tyk**.
sentence.en: The book has many pages, so it is very thick.

tynd.explanation: "Tynd" means "thin", for a book, a layer, a slice or a piece of cloth. It also describes watery liquids, such as "tynd suppe" (thin soup). About a person it can sound negative; "slank" (slim) is the kinder word.

sentence.da: Bogen har kun få sider, så den er meget **tynd**.
sentence.en: The book has only a few pages, so it is very thin.

tyrkiet.explanation: "Tyrkiet" means "Turkey", the country. The bird is "en kalkun" (a turkey).

sentence.da: Istanbul er en stor by i **Tyrkiet**.
sentence.en: Istanbul is a big city in Turkey.

tyrkisk.explanation: "Tyrkisk" means "Turkish", for people, things and the language. It is written with a small letter, where English writes "Turkish" with a capital.

sentence.da: Hun kommer fra Tyrkiet og taler **tyrkisk**.
sentence.en: She comes from Turkey and speaks Turkish.

tysk.explanation: "Tysk" means "German", for things from Germany and for the language. It is written with a small letter, where English writes "German" with a capital. "At tale tysk" means "to speak German".

sentence.da: Han kommer fra Tyskland og taler **tysk**.
sentence.en: He comes from Germany and speaks German.

tyskland.explanation: "Tyskland" means "Germany". It is made of "tysk" (German) and "land" (country).

sentence.da: Berlin er en stor by i **Tyskland**.
sentence.en: Berlin is a big city in Germany.

tyve.explanation: "Tyve" means "twenty". In numbers like 21 the ones come first: "enogtyve" is literally "one-and-twenty", and 22 is "toogtyve" ("two-and-twenty").

sentence.da: Ti og ti er **tyve**.
sentence.en: Ten and ten is twenty.

tåge.explanation: "Tåge" means "fog", the low cloud that makes it hard to see. Danish says "der er tåge" (there is fog) where English says "it is foggy".

sentence.da: Der er **tåge**, så jeg kan ikke se bilen foran mig.
sentence.en: There is fog, so I cannot see the car in front of me.

tæt på.explanation: "Tæt på" means "close to", and the place comes after it: "tæt på stationen" (close to the station). On its own it means "close by".

sentence.da: Hotellet ligger **tæt på** stranden.
sentence.en: The hotel is close to the beach.

tøj.explanation: "Tøj" means "clothes". It has no plural: you say "mit tøj" (my clothes) or "noget tøj" (some clothes). One item has its own name, such as "en trøje" (a sweater).

sentence.da: Bukser, trøjer og jakker er alt sammen **tøj**.
sentence.en: Trousers, sweaters and jackets are all clothes.

tør.explanation: "Tør" means "dry", for clothes, weather, skin or bread. Do not mix it up with "tør" in "jeg tør ikke" (I dare not): it is a different word that looks the same.

sentence.da: Jakken var våd, men nu er den **tør**.
sentence.en: The jacket was wet, but now it is dry.

tørstig.explanation: "Tørstig" means "thirsty". "Jeg er tørstig" means "I am thirsty". Danes also say "Jeg har tørst", literally "I have thirst".

sentence.da: Jeg er **tørstig**, så jeg drikker et glas vand.
sentence.en: I am thirsty, so I drink a glass of water.
